title: Nanoelectromechanical relay access switch with air-gap zero leakage
idea: Po: the access transistor is always perfectly off. Replace the access FET with a vertical NEM relay whose cantilever is pulled onto the storage-node contact by the wordline field and springs back to leave a ~5 nm air gap, so off-state leakage is only gap tunneling (<1e-21 A); a low-adhesion RuO2 contact and pull-in/pull-out hysteresis keep the wordline swing under ~1 V.
why: Fact 3 leakage tail: removes subthreshold, GIDL and junction paths so retention is set by the capacitor dielectric alone; refresh interval could go from 64 ms to minutes (>1000x less refresh energy). Risk: 1e15-cycle contact endurance and ns mechanical switching.

title: Resonant charge-recycling refresh through on-package LC tank
idea: Po: refresh pays for itself. During refresh bursts, bitline and wordline charge is swung adiabatically by a resonant inductor-capacitor tank (inductor built into the interposer) instead of being dumped to ground, so energy spent restoring one row is mostly recovered into the next row's precharge.
why: Fact 3 (~46 fJ/bit refresh) and fact 10 (CV^2 floor): adiabatic stepping cuts refresh energy 3-5x without touching the cell.

title: Self-healing tail cells via localized Joule anneal of junction traps
idea: Po: the leakiest cell sets the refresh, so the leakiest cell must heal itself. On-die BIST finds the worst-retention cells and drives a controlled forward current through their storage-node junction, self-heating it to ~400 C for microseconds so hydrogen/deuterium from a reservoir liner re-passivates the trap that causes the tail.
why: Fact 3: refresh rate is set by the <0.01% tail; compressing the tail 4-8x allows ~4x longer refresh interval, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~75%.

title: Route chilled-water inlet to DRAM first for retention-tiered cooling
idea: Po: DRAM lives in a refrigerator. Re-plumb liquid-cooled AI racks so the coldest inlet water (~15 C) crosses DRAM cold plates before the GPUs, holding arrays near 25 C instead of 85 C, and have the controller apply temperature-compensated refresh tables that stretch tREFI as leakage halves every ~10 C.
why: Fact 3: junction leakage falls ~30-60x from 85 C to 25 C, so refresh interval can stretch 8-16x, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax and idle refresh power at near-zero capex.

title: Per-cell threshold trimming via charge-trap layer in access gate
idea: Po: every access transistor is custom-made. Add a thin SiN charge-trap film inside the buried-wordline gate stack; at wafer test, cells in the leakage tail receive a one-time Fowler-Nordheim program pulse that raises their Vt ~150 mV, tightening the Vt distribution until the tail disappears.
why: Fact 3: a 10x tighter off-current tail lets refresh run 4-8x less often and permits a shallower negative wordline, saving refresh energy and charge-pump area (fact 7).

title: Negative-capacitance gate stack enabling 1.5 V wordline access transistor
idea: Po: the gate amplifies its own voltage. Insert a thin doped-HfO2 negative-capacitance layer in series with the access gate dielectric so subthreshold swing drops below 60 mV/dec in the operating window, letting the wordline swing about -0.3 to 1.5 V instead of -0.5 to 3 V at the same on/off ratio.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor and fact 3: halving wordline swing cuts wordline CV^2 ~4x, shrinks the pumps (fact 7) and adds ~10x off-current margin.

title: Decaying reference cells make sense threshold slide with leakage
idea: Po: the reference forgets as fast as the data. Each subarray carries reference cells written to a half level at the same time as the row and sharing its well, so they leak at the same rate; the sense amp compares against this decaying reference instead of a fixed VBL/2, so a decayed 1 still reads correctly long after it crossed the fixed midpoint.
why: Fact 3: sensing margin, not total charge loss, sets retention; a tracking reference extends usable retention 2-3x and cuts refresh energy and bandwidth tax proportionally.

title: Sense-amp latch-time telemetry skips refresh for healthy rows
idea: Po: every read is a medical exam. A tiny time-to-digital converter on the local sense amps measures how fast each activated row resolves (faster = more charge left); rows with ample margin set a skip counter so their next one or two scheduled refreshes are dropped, and VRT cells are caught in the act.
why: Fact 3: measured rather than worst-case retention lets 70-90% of refreshes be skipped under real workloads, returning bandwidth and idle power.

title: Refresh-off KV-cache zones with recompute-on-ECC-fail
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. LLM serving runtimes tag KV-cache and activation pages as decay-tolerant; the controller places those banks in a ~1 s refresh mode, and when on-die ECC flags an uncorrectable block the runtime recomputes that token's keys and values from the prompt instead of faulting.
why: Fact 3: KV cache is often 30-60% of inference DRAM; cutting its refresh 16x removes most refresh energy there and returns bandwidth to compute.

title: Vacuum-channel field-emission nanotriode as DRAM access device
idea: Po: the transistor channel is empty. Build the access device as a sealed ~10 nm vacuum gap between a sharp emitter tip on the bitline side and the storage node, gated by a wordline ring; electrons cross only when the gate field thins the emission barrier, so the off state has no semiconductor, no junction and no GIDL.
why: Fact 3: eliminates every semiconductor leakage path, enabling refresh intervals of seconds, plus radiation hardness; risk is emission uniformity and tip wear at nanoscale.

title: Gallium-oxide thin-film access transistors with 4.8 eV bandgap
idea: Po: the access transistor is made from an insulator. Deposit Ga2O3 by low-temperature ALD with laser crystallization as the access channel; its 4.8 eV gap makes thermal generation negligible, targeting off-current near 1e-21 A per cell, well below IGZO.
why: Fact 3: ~100x lower tail than IGZO and ~1e7x below Si, allowing hour-scale refresh and smaller capacitors (fact 1); risk is ~10 cm2/Vs mobility and contact resistance.

title: Series dual-wordline vertical access with stack-effect leakage and AND addressing
idea: Po: every lock needs two keys. Put two independently driven gate rings in series on one vertical pillar channel, one on a row wordline and one on a column-group wordline; the cell opens only when both are high, so off leakage falls by the stack effect and half-selected cells see only one gate on.
why: Facts 3 and 9: stack effect cuts subthreshold leakage 10-30x and splits the drain field to curb GIDL; AND-addressing also blunts row hammer because an aggressor wordline only half-opens its neighbors.

title: Rescue scrapped dies with per-row refresh maps sold as SKU
idea: Po: the trash bin is a warehouse. Dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen because a few hundred rows are weak get a per-row refresh-class map burned into on-die fuses; the module controller refreshes those rows at 16-32 ms and the rest normally, and the parts ship as a mapped-refresh grade.
why: Usable supply: recovering 3-8% of output lost to retention fallout adds bits with no new fab, at <1% bandwidth cost.

title: Regulatory idle-watts-per-terabyte metric forcing refresh-aware servers
idea: Po: refresh is illegal. Add a measured idle-memory-watts-per-TB line to server efficiency rules and large procurement specs (ENERGY STAR, EU ecodesign, federal data-center buys), tested in self-refresh, so vendors must ship temperature-compensated refresh, partial-array self-refresh and OS free-page hints enabled by default.
why: Fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle DRAM power; scoring it pushes features already in silicon into deployment, cutting fleet refresh energy 2-4x.

title: Dangling-bond-free 2D channel removes interface-trap leakage tail
idea: Po: the channel has no surface. Wrap a WSe2 or MoS2 monolayer channel around the pillar with an hBN gate dielectric so there are no dangling bonds at the channel interface, leaving the trap-assisted tunneling that creates the leakage tail and variable retention time with no sites to act through.
why: Fact 3: the tail and VRT are trap-driven; a trap-free channel could tighten the off-current distribution ~100x and extend refresh interval ~10x.

title: Free-page hints stop refresh of unallocated rows
idea: Po: memory only remembers what someone cares about. The OS streams its free-page bitmap to the DRAM controller via a new mode-register/CXL command; rows whose pages are all free are dropped from the refresh rotation and are zero-initialized on next allocation.
why: Fact 3: servers often hold 20-50% free or clean-cache memory; skipping it cuts refresh energy and bandwidth tax proportionally.

title: Compress rows and pad with discharged cells that cannot decay
idea: Po: most memory is empty. The controller compresses each row, writes the payload into the fewest cells, fills the rest with the discharged state (which in true cells cannot leak into an error) and picks per-row polarity so most bits sit in the safe state; rows flagged all-safe skip refresh.
why: Fact 3: only charged cells need refresh; with ~2x compressibility and polarity choice, 50-70% of charged cells vanish and many rows skip refresh entirely.

title: OS compacts live pages into best-retention rows before self-refresh
idea: Po: the best cells do all the work. On entering idle, the OS migrates live pages into rows profiled as the top-decile retention class and powers the rest down with partial-array self-refresh, so the self-refresh interval is set by the best rows, not the worst.
why: Fact 3 idle power: best-decile rows retain ~10x longer than the worst, so standby refresh power in phones and edge boxes drops up to ~10x.

title: Substrate removal by back-side thinning eliminates junction leakage paths
idea: Po: the chip has no floor. After front-end processing, bond the DRAM wafer face-down to a carrier and remove the bulk silicon so access transistors sit in a fully depleted thin body on oxide, deleting the storage-node-to-substrate junction and the substrate holes that feed leakage.
why: Fact 3: junction and substrate-driven tail mechanisms disappear (3-10x tail reduction); the exposed back side also hosts a bias/power plane, freeing periphery area (fact 7).

title: Bottom-up grown nanowire channels with etch-free sidewalls
idea: Po: chips are grown, not made. Grow single-crystal Si access channels inside the pillar openings by selective epitaxy or tin-catalyzed VLS instead of etching them out of the wafer, so the channel sidewalls carry no plasma-etch damage, the dominant source of trap-assisted leakage in vertical access devices.
why: Facts 3 and 2: a damage-free channel tightens the tail and makes vertical 4F^2 access viable without its usual leakage penalty.

title: Constant-bias field plate over storage junction suppresses GIDL
idea: Po: the drain sees no electric field. Split the buried wordline into an active gate over the channel and a separate field-plate segment over the storage-node overlap held at a fixed mild positive bias, so the gate-to-drain field that drives band-to-band GIDL never forms even while the active gate sits at negative hold.
why: Fact 3: GIDL is a main tail mechanism under negative wordline; removing it allows deeper negative hold and 3-5x lower tail leakage.

title: Lazy refresh with LDPC resurrection across row groups
idea: Po: let bits die, then resurrect them. Refresh 8x less often and protect each group of 8 rows with a soft-decision LDPC code whose parity sits in a spare row; sense amps report a soft confidence level, and the decoder rewrites corrected data on read, treating decay as a noisy channel.
why: Fact 3: an 8x longer interval cuts refresh energy ~85% and returns 10-20% bandwidth for ~6% capacity overhead.

title: Photoconductive access switch opened by waveguide light pulses
idea: Po: the switch is opened by light. Replace the access transistor with an a-Si:H or chalcogenide photoconductor between bitline and storage node; the wordline is a silicon-nitride waveguide, and a light pulse makes the row conductive for nanoseconds, while in the dark leakage is bulk dark current (aA) with no gate, no GIDL and no wordline voltage.
why: Facts 3 and 10: no 3 V wordline and no GIDL, with dark-current-limited leakage allowing minute-scale refresh; risk is photoconductor speed and optical power per row.

title: Hole quantum-well floating body in SiGe for long retention
idea: Po: the stored charge lives in a room with no exit. Build a capacitorless floating-body cell with a buried compressively strained SiGe layer under the channel whose valence-band offset traps holes in a quantum well, so stored holes cannot recombine through the source/drain junctions as fast as in plain silicon.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor (4F^2 possible) while band confinement lifts floating-body retention from ~10 ms toward >1 s, cutting refresh 50-100x.

title: Direct-tunneling charge-trap gate memory with seconds retention
idea: Po: the transistor remembers its own gate. Store the bit as electrons in a SiN trap layer above a 1.5-2 nm tunnel oxide; writes use direct tunneling at ~2 V in tens of ns with no hot carriers, so per-cycle damage is tiny, while retention is seconds rather than years, making a refresh-lite capacitorless DRAM.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor, and refresh 15x rarer than 64 ms; the risk is reaching 1e15 endurance.

title: Pulsed-hold thyristor array refreshed blindly without sense amplifiers
idea: Po: refresh without reading. Use vertical gated thyristor latches (no capacitor) but power their anode lines only in short pulses; between pulses an ON cell's base charge decays slowly, and each pulse re-latches every ON cell in the array at once while OFF cells stay off.
why: Fact 3: refresh needs no activate, sense or restore, so it uses no bitline charge or bandwidth, and duty cycling cuts thyristor standby power 10-100x.

title: Bistable buckled nanobeam storing bits by mechanical position
idea: Po: the bit is a shape. Each cell is a pre-stressed buckled nanobeam (TiN or amorphous carbon) clamped at both ends and resting in one of two curved states; electrostatic pulses from two side electrodes snap it between states, and its position is read by tunnel current to a sense electrode.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no leakage-limited retention, so refresh is zero; risk is snap speed (~ns at 100 nm) and fatigue over 1e15 cycles.

title: Antiferroelectric gate with built-in bias trades retention for endurance
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Put a ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric layer in the gate stack of a single transistor with asymmetric work-function electrodes that shift its loop so one polarized state is metastable for ~1 s; the field-induced phase relaxes back on its own, giving a refreshed volatile 1T bit with much less fatigue than full ferroelectric switching.
why: Facts 1 and 3: capacitorless bit with refresh ~15x rarer than DRAM, aiming at 1e14+ endurance; goes beyond the prior nonvolatile HZO work.

title: Deliberately low-barrier MTJs as refreshed fast spin DRAM
idea: Po: a magnet that is supposed to forget. Design MTJ free layers with only ~25 kT energy barrier so bits flip spontaneously after ~10-100 ms; the low barrier cuts write current ~10x, so a minimum access device suffices, and bits are scrubbed on a DRAM-like refresh schedule.
why: Facts 1 and 10: no capacitor, low write voltage, ~10 fJ writes and effectively unlimited endurance since the barrier is never stressed; beyond prior nonvolatile MRAM.

title: Proton-intercalation transistor storing bits as channel conductance
idea: Po: the bit is a pH. Each cell is a three-terminal electrochemical transistor: a gate pulse pushes protons from a solid electrolyte (HfO2:H) into a MoO3 or SmNiO3 channel (avoiding the tungsten chokepoint), shifting its conductance; reading channel current is nondestructive and retention runs seconds to hours with no capacitor.
why: Facts 3 and 8: nondestructive read removes restore and overfetch penalties and long retention cuts refresh; risk is ns proton motion and endurance.

title: Erasable conductive ferroelectric domain walls as nondestructive bits
idea: Po: the wire appears and disappears. In a thin-film lithium niobate cell, a pulse between two side electrodes nucleates a charged domain wall that conducts ~1e4x better than the bulk, and an opposite pulse erases it; reading wall current is nondestructive, so the bit needs neither capacitor nor refresh.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 8: no capacitor, refresh or restore, with ns domain switching; risk is LiNbO3-on-Si integration and wall current at 20 nm.

title: Van der Waals semi-floating-gate cell with hBN tunnel window
idea: Po: the storage node is a sheet of graphite. Stack MoS2 channel / hBN / multilayer graphene floating gate, where the floating gate also touches the drain through a thin WSe2 p-n junction window: writes inject charge through the junction in ~ns at 1-2 V, hBN holds it for seconds, and read senses the channel nondestructively.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 8: no capacitor, nondestructive read and retention far beyond 64 ms; risk is wafer-scale 2D stacking.

title: Complementary tunnel-FET static latch with attoamp hold current
idea: Po: SRAM that costs nothing to hold. Build a 4T cross-coupled latch from complementary vertical tunnel FETs whose band-to-band off-current is ~1e-17 A, monolithically stacked in two tiers over the access tier so a bit occupies ~8F^2; data is held statically and refresh disappears.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh, with standby near mW per GB; risk is TFET on-current (read speed) and tier-stacking density.

title: Vertical 3D charge-coupled shift-register memory with one regenerator per string
idea: Po: the bit is a rumor passed down a line. Store charge packets in potential wells along a tall vertical channel with dozens of stacked gate layers (3D NAND-like tiers clocked as a CCD); packets shift up and down and only the end-of-string regenerating sense amp restores them, so refresh is the shifting itself, with no per-bit capacitor or access transistor.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: reuses 3D NAND tier deposition (no EUV per tier, density scales with tier count); access becomes 100 ns-1 us block access, suited to tensor streams.

title: Compiler-proven tensor lifetimes shorter than retention need zero refresh
idea: Po: data dies before it decays. In AI training, activations and gradients live ~1-10 ms between write and last read; the compiler proves each tensor's lifetime and places it in capacitorless floating-body memory with ~10 ms retention that is never refreshed, while long-lived weights go elsewhere.
why: Facts 1 and 3: lets a cheap, poor-retention capacitorless cell serve 40-60% of training memory with zero refresh energy.

title: Engineered single border trap per cell as atomic-scale bit
idea: Po: the defect that causes leakage is the memory. Place one deep border trap per minimum-size transistor by single-ion implantation and use its occupancy, which shifts Vt by tens of mV in a ~10 nm device just as random telegraph noise does, as the stored bit; write by gate-bias pulse, read by drain current.
why: Facts 1 and 3: the smallest conceivable capacitorless cell, with retention set by trap emission time (designable ms to s); speculative because single-trap placement and read margin are hard.

title: AlGaN/GaN polarization well storing floating 2DEG charge for days
idea: Po: the electron is locked in a polarization cage. Use a floating AlGaN/GaN island as the gate of a read transistor; the polarization-induced 2DEG well in 3.4 eV GaN holds electrons with negligible thermal generation for days, written through a thin AlN tunnel barrier.
why: Facts 1 and 3 plus U.S. manufacturability (GaN-on-Si lines exist domestically): quasi-nonvolatile capacitorless storage cuts refresh ~1000x.

title: Read-restoring gain cell where every read tops up storage node
idea: Po: reading is refreshing. In a 2T capacitorless gain cell, add a diode-connected feedback from the read path so read current through a 1 cell briefly pulls its storage gate back toward full level, while a 0 cell draws no current and stays low; any row read regularly never needs a separate refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 8: hot rows refresh themselves for free and reads stay nondestructive; with typical access patterns 50%+ of refreshes vanish.

title: Capacitorless gain-cell memory tiles from mature U.S. logic fabs
idea: Po: memory made in a factory that has never made a capacitor. License a 3T silicon gain cell on 22-28 nm logic processes at existing U.S. foundries and sell it as memory tiles hybrid-bonded under accelerators, hiding its ~1 ms retention with retention-aware refresh, with no capacitor module, EUV or DRAM fab needed.
why: Fact 4 and capital: uses depreciated U.S. logic capacity (near-zero new capex) for near-compute buffers, offloading 10-20% of HBM demand.

title: Convert DRAM capacitor-module tool bays into capacitorless 3D tiers
idea: Po: the fab throws away its capacitor tools. In an existing DRAM fab, retire the high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch, high-k and TiN modules and reuse the bays for stacked capacitorless floating-body tiers built from epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattices, leaving the periphery line unchanged.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: removes the 60-75:1 etch and ~15-20% of process steps and turns sunk fab space into 3D capacity years faster than a new fab.

title: Ferroelectric-semiconductor alpha-In2Se3 channel as its own memory
idea: Po: the channel remembers which way it points. Make the transistor channel from the ferroelectric semiconductor alpha-In2Se3, whose out-of-plane polarization flips with a gate pulse and modulates channel conductance; there is no separate ferroelectric layer or capacitor, and read is nondestructive.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 8: capacitorless, refresh-free, nondestructive low-voltage bit beyond the HZO prior; risk is endurance and CMOS-compatible In2Se3 deposition.

title: Parametric phase bits in high-Q nanomechanical resonators
idea: Po: the bit is a rhythm, not a charge. Revive Goto's parametron: each cell is a nanomechanical resonator pumped at twice its natural frequency, which settles into oscillation at phase 0 or pi; the phase is the bit, held while the shared pump runs, written by a seed pulse and read by a phase detector.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no leakage decay; the shared pump replaces refresh; speculative on density and pump power per bit.

title: Coulomb-blockade few-electron dot in axial nanowire heterostructure
idea: Po: the bit is ten electrons that cannot leave. Grow vertical nanowires with an axial Ge dot between two thin wide-gap barriers; Coulomb blockade plus band offset make adding or removing electrons a quantized step written by a gate pulse, and the dot charge gates the nanowire channel beneath it for readout.
why: Facts 1 and 3: one nanowire (~4F^2) per cell with no capacitor; barrier-set retention could reach seconds; speculative at room temperature.

title: Goto-pair tunnel-diode static cell with picoamp valley hold
idea: Po: two leaks fight and the bit is whoever wins. Series-connect two nanoscale Esaki tunnel diodes as a Goto pair between rails so their negative-differential-resistance curves cross at two stable points; the midpoint node holds the bit statically behind one access transistor, with standby set by valley current scaled to pA.
why: Facts 1 and 3: capacitorless static storage with no refresh; ~8F^2 if diodes stack vertically; risk is valley current and peak-current uniformity.

title: Ovonic threshold switch recovery-time as a volatile crosspoint bit
idea: Po: the selector remembers that it just fired. After an ovonic threshold switch turns on, its threshold stays lowered for ms before recovering; write a 1 by firing the cell, then read with a pulse between the lowered and recovered thresholds so only recently fired cells conduct, giving a capacitorless, transistorless 4F^2 crosspoint DRAM where refresh means re-firing.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: stackable BEOL crosspoint tiers with no capacitor or access transistor; speculative on retention control and read disturb.

title: Milestone prize for capacitorless 4F^2 cell meeting DRAM spec
idea: Po: the government bans capacitors. Fund a U.S. prize with staged payouts: $50M for a capacitorless 4F^2 cell holding 64 ms at 85 C on 300 mm wafers, $200M for a 1 Gb array at 1e15 endurance made in a domestic fab, with IP licensed to all U.S. makers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: pulls many capacitorless paths forward in parallel for a few hundred million dollars instead of a $15B fab.
